ingredients.h2: Four named, one of them not a species
ingredients.intro: The listing names four plants and calls the remainder a proprietary blend. Three of the four can be pinned to a binomial with reasonable confidence. The fourth, chamomile, is a word that covers two different plants, and the listing does not say which, so this page does not say either. We hold no photograph of any of them, so those frames are empty rather than filled with a stand-in, and any picture on this page that is a generated scene says so.

cards.p: A small tropical tree of the Caribbean and of Central and South America, now grown across the tropics, carrying a heavy green fruit covered in soft curved spines. The fruit is eaten fresh and pulped for drinks; the dried leaf is what is usually sold in the herb trade as graviola. Which part of the tree is in this jar is not printed.

Two different plants are sold under this name. Matricaria chamomilla, called German chamomile or scented mayweed, is an annual of European field edges and disturbed ground. Chamaemelum nobile, Roman chamomile, is a low creeping perennial of western Europe. Same family, different genus, different plant. The listing prints the English word and no binomial, so we print no binomial either. The dried flower head is the part sold in both cases.

A tall perennial of damp ground and riverbank through Europe and into western Asia, with divided leaves and a flat head of pale pink flowers. The root and rhizome are the parts usually sold, and they carry a smell that everybody notices and few people enjoy. The listing prints the common name only; this is the species the word covers in the trade. Older books put the genus in a family of its own, Valerianaceae, since folded into Caprifoliaceae. The caution that travels with this plant is on the sheet below.

A tall perennial of wet meadow, ditch and streamside across North America, with narrow toothed leaves and candelabra spikes of small blue-purple flowers that open in a ring working upward. The name blue vervain belongs to this species; plain vervain usually means Verbena officinalis, a different European plant entirely. The aerial parts are what is usually gathered. The listing prints the common name only.

cards.common: No plant in it is printed
cards.p: Whatever else is in the capsule appears on the listing as a proprietary blend of herbs and nothing further. The phrase means the label is not telling you. It is the one row on this sheet nobody can fill in, and it stays empty until the label prints the plants.

Valerian products sold in this country carry a standard warning that they may make you drowsy: if you are affected, do not drive or use machinery, and that warning applies to this jar. Food supplements should not be used as a substitute for a varied and balanced diet and a healthy lifestyle. Keep out of reach of young children.

doctrine.h3: We publish the specification. We do not publish claims about what it does.
doctrine.p: Three of the four plants are pinned to a binomial here, the fourth is left as the English word the listing prints, the serving and the schedule are printed, and the two figures nobody has measured are marked missing rather than filled in. Neptune is the name on the jar. It is a name, not a description, and we do not expand it. What any of these plants does in a body is not something we are permitted to say, so it is not on this page.

reiss.label: Reiss's turn
paras: Chamomile is on this listing with nothing after it, and that is not a small omission. Two different plants are sold under the word. Matricaria chamomilla is an annual of European field edges. Chamaemelum nobile is a low creeping perennial. Same family, different genus, and no way at all to tell from a label that just says chamomile.

I could pick one. Most people writing a page like this would take the commoner of the two, put it in italics, and nobody would ever query it. I do not know which is in the jar, and a Latin name invented for a label is worse than an English one printed honestly.

The storage line on the listing says to store it away from radiation. I cannot act on that and neither can you, so the sheet above carries the plain instruction instead and says what it replaced. I would rather show you the edit than make it quietly.

The valerian warning is standard on every valerian product sold in this country and it is on the sheet for the same reason the stop date is on Decolonise. A limit printed plainly is worth more to somebody at a counter than a paragraph of reassurance.
reiss.pull: A Latin name invented for a label is worse than an English one printed honestly.
